title: ai knows everything, so why does its raw output feel like nothing?
author: FotoRe_store
selftext:
every day here someone argues if ai games are art or slop, and theres a huge thread in r/gamedev now about if code is art. i think the problem is people treat art like a yes or no thing. for me art is creativity that takes in some context, and that context can be small or huge. a game you make for your kid takes in the context of your kid, your jokes, your evenings together. thats real art, just small. great art takes in the context of a whole generation or an epoch

and if you look from the side of the person who plays or watches, its like the thing lays a path through their brain, through connections they already have, but linking them in a way they would never link them alone. the more unexpected and bright that path is the more special the thing is. but it has to be a path you can actually walk. random noise lights up a lot of stuff too but goes nowhere. and a too predictable path is like a highway you drove a thousand times, you dont even notice it

the author cant see inside your head, only his own. so he lays the path by feel through himself and hopes you have similar places inside. thats why a game for your own kid hits so hard, your maps are almost the same. and great art somehow finds places almost everyone has. and the path stays after, you walk away a bit different. when the same path gets laid in millions of heads it becomes part of the context of the time, and the next artists take it in

now ai. a model took in more context than any human ever, the whole civilization basically. so why does its raw output feel empty? i think because it gives you the average of all of it. thats the highway path again. it becomes art exactly as much as a person squeezes it with choices, picks this, throws that away, insists on something weird. so a homemade ai game for your kid can be real small art, and it also explains why so many posts here feel the same

i was thinking this through in a long talk with claude. curious if it matches how you feel about your own stuff

comments.author: ArtificialImages
comments.body:
It will give you the minimum it thinks you'll accept. 

Basically it thinks you're dumb and you need to show it otherwise.

What are you using? How are you using it? What results do you get?

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: claude opus, in the normal chat on purpose, because for me talking things through matters as much as the code. i dont code at all. how: i describe what i want, ask for sketches, usually 2 to 6 versions as pictures, pick one or mix them, then it builds and i test on my phones and send it the logs. and yes about the minimum, the first version is almost always the average, the good stuff comes after many rounds. result is a browser game you control with your palm in the air, the phone works as a sonar. its open source if you want to see how it was made

comments.author: frogic
comments.body:
So you make connections based on the set memories and experience of your brain and then try to figure out the solution to your problem.  Then you take the feedback you get either from halfway making it and externally or your own intuition and then you iterate on that until you like it.  An llm has a huge context.  Neccesarily larger but in the specifics of something like game design or coding definitely larger than the vast majority of us.  It then takes the input from your chat, harness, and repo and does basically the same thing.  Then it goes to either you or depending on your setup another agent with its own context to fix it.  Eventually you go through and make changes.  So all of that process is similar.

Now here's the magic part: You're able to tweek its most important (system level) instructions to mold its output towards what you want.  You of course can give small notes or tell it to try again with a different approach but also if the general style/vision of your game isn't right you can set rules and guards in a way that causes more of a symbiotic relationship with you.  Every conversation about the purpose or style of your game should be updating memories and guideline files that influence every decision.  You'll even notice that in your conversations with claude.  The llm is always trying to predict what you want it to say.  Its not actually solving problems in the way you think of it its trying to have the correct next token so any conversation where you have an opinion unless you write lots of guardrails to make it push back on you.

Obviously this implies you care what the llm produces and have a specific idea for your game.  You can always go 'make me a robot' and it will and it will make the next robot based on that and so on.  So it requires effort from you and a resistance to the llm gaslighting you away from what you want.  Another fun part of this is that one of the best ways to avoid your llm to making the same generic thing is to ask it how to do that because the first lesson about llm's is they understand themselves better than you can.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: yeah thats pretty much how it works for me. i keep notes that every new session reads, with my decisions, and also a list of things i already rejected so it doesnt offer them again. honestly the rejected list is maybe the most useful file. about pushing back, it does if you ask it to check with data instead of opinions. once i was sure the ship was slowly drifting away from my hand during a game, it went through the game log and showed me there was no drift at all, just normal wobble. another time i wanted the phone to turn the volume up when the echo is weak, and the logs showed the real reason was my hand being further away, not the volume. so i think these notes and rules are exactly the squeezing i wrote about, without them you just get the highway

comments.author: Fizassist1
comments.body: the only reason game dev is debating if code is art, is because nobody can agree on what to hate with whats created with ai.  people saying code is art are the same people saying AI in game development is always bad.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: i think thats a big part of it. as long as art is a yes or no label it works like a weapon, you call your side art and the other side slop and then its fine to hate it. thats kind of why i like thinking about it as a radius. then you just ask how far it reaches and whose choices squeezed it, and that question works the same for code, pictures, music and ai stuff
